title: Americans Born After 1970 Are Dying Faster Than Their Parents Did. The Data Is Alarming.
excerpt: A Tufts University study tracking 45 years of mortality data reveals that Gen Xers and elder millennials face rising death rates from heart disease, cancer, and drug overdoses — reversing a century of progress that many immigrant families took for granted.
body:
For most of the twentieth century, being born American meant you would probably outlive your parents. Each generation cleared a slightly higher bar — better medicine, cleaner water, fewer infectious diseases, longer lives. It was so reliable that demographers treated it almost as a law of nature.

That law has broken.

A sweeping new analysis published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reveals that Americans born after 1970 — late Gen Xers and elder millennials, now in their thirties and forties — are dying at higher rates from heart disease, cancer, and external causes than the generations before them did at the same age. The reversal is not subtle. It is broad, it is accelerating, and it has been building for decades.

The 1950s Turning Point

The research, led by social epidemiologist Leah Abrams of Tufts University, tracks 45 years of American mortality data from 1979 to 2023. The team analysed death certificate records for birth cohorts stretching from the 1890s to the 1980s, across three major cause-of-death categories: cardiovascular disease, cancer, and external causes including drug overdoses, suicides, homicides, and traffic accidents.

What emerged was a clear inflection point. Americans born in the 1940s experienced steady, measurable improvements in survival at every stage of life. Those born in the 1950s saw that progress slow. And for those born after 1970, the trend reversed outright.

"We see concerning trends for those born from around 1970 to 1985 — the late Gen Xers and elder millennials," Abrams said. "These cohorts are trending worse than their predecessors in all-cause mortality; deaths from cardiovascular disease and cancer, especially colon cancer; and external causes."

Two Crises, Not One

The study identifies two distinct forces dragging American life expectancy backward. The first is generational: newer cohorts are entering middle age carrying more risk factors — obesity, sedentary lifestyles, metabolic disease, substance dependence — than any generation before them.

The second is a broad, period-based deterioration that began around 2010 and has affected nearly all living adult cohorts simultaneously. This wave, driven primarily by cardiovascular disease mortality and the opioid crisis, has layered itself on top of the generational decline, compounding the damage.

The result is a unique predicament. Unlike past mortality crises that had identifiable, single causes — a war, a pandemic, a famine — America's current life expectancy stagnation is multifaceted. Heart disease, cancer, drug overdoses, and suicide are all rising among the young, fed by overlapping social, economic, and biological forces.

The Colon Cancer Signal

One finding stood out even to the researchers. Deaths from colon cancer are rising sharply among younger generations — a trend that tracks with the broader epidemic of early-onset colorectal cancer that has made headlines in recent years.

"Greater cancer prevalence can indicate that we're simply catching cancer sooner," Abrams noted. "But our study shows increased mortality, and it's never good to have more deaths at young ages. This is a genuinely alarming trend."

The study links the increase to growing problems with obesity and ultra-processed diets — the same dietary shift that has reshaped American eating habits over the past four decades and disproportionately affects communities with limited access to fresh food.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the millions of Indians who immigrated to the United States expecting better health outcomes, this data complicates the narrative. The American healthcare system remains technologically advanced, but the society around it is producing sicker people faster than medicine can keep up.

First-generation immigrants often carry a health advantage — the so-called "healthy immigrant effect" — driven by active lifestyles and traditional diets. But their children, raised on American food systems and sedentary routines, may not inherit that protection.

The study's findings are particularly sobering for South Asian families already managing elevated genetic risks for heart disease and diabetes. A generation of NRI children and young adults, born and raised in the US between the 1980s and 2000s, falls squarely into the cohorts the study identifies as most at risk.

There is one bright note in the data. The study confirmed that past public health interventions — especially tobacco control — produced significant, lasting reductions in mortality. Smoking-related cancer and cardiovascular deaths declined sharply across cohorts that came of age after anti-smoking campaigns took hold, proving that population-level interventions can bend these curves.

Whether America has the political will to mount a comparable campaign against obesity, ultra-processed food, and the opioid crisis remains an open question. For diaspora families, the takeaway is more personal: the health advantages that first-generation immigrants brought with them are not automatic. They have to be actively, deliberately passed on.
